title: Lumos Orchestrate - Vendor Exit & Compatibility Scout
summary: Initial migration scout. Lumos is exploring an exit from a mixed OpenAI + self-hosted vLLM/TGI stack toward a unified inference platform. Primary concerns: latency/cost parity, security and data residency, KV cache semantics, private VPC routing, and auditability for compliance. AE/SE outlined hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs and proposed an eval plan (benchmarks + sample prompts + canary rollout). Next: share benchmark template, security pack, and schedule a 1-week workload parity run with telemetry.
topics: Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs
action_items: Maya Patel - Send benchmark spreadsheet + sample prompt set - 2028-12-10
Jonah Reed - Prepare runtime parity checklist (vLLM/TGI kernel notes) - 2028-12-12
Ethan Wu - Share current traffic profiles and top 200 prompts (anonymized) - 2028-12-11
Priya Menon - Provide example model configs, quantization details - 2028-12-13
Carlos Diaz - Confirm network constraints for Private VPC testing - 2028-12-14
next_steps: Redwood to provision a 1-week Dedicated eval pool (estimate) and provide telemetry hooks
Customer to supply prompt set and perf traces
Schedule technical deep dive focused on KV cache semantics and prefix caching
Share security pack (SOC2, ISO, SSO guides, KMS integration docs)
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2028-12-07 14:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reed (Redwood SE), Ethan Wu (CTO - Lumos), Priya Menon (ML Eng), Carlos Diaz (SRE), Marina Holt (Legal), Samir Rao (Product)

Summary (auto): initial scoping call for vendor exit/compatibility. Discussed parity requirements and evaluation plan.

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick us off. quick intros?
[00:08] Ethan Wu: Ethan - CTO at Lumos, we run a hybrid stack right now; some production on OpenAI for chat, and we recently rolled our own inference using vLLM + TGI for lower cost batched workloads.
[00:17] Priya Menon: priya here, ML engineer, i've been working on the vLLM throughput tuning and we see some weird kv cache misses when sequences warm up.
[00:25] Jonah Reed: okay that makes sense, kv cache behavior is a frequent differentiator. Jonah from Redwood, i look at runtime optimizations.
[00:31] Carlos Diaz: SRE - i'm focused on networking and compliance, esp private VPC needs.
[00:35] Maya Patel: high level today — figure out if Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private can meet your parity goals and what an eval would look like. also capture security asks so we can loop legal.

[02:00] Ethan Wu: main drivers: cost predictability and staying off the public provider for some PII workloads. we also need parity on latency and output quality — we can't regress.
[02:12] Samir Rao: product is worried about hallucinations increasing after migration, so eval needs to measure quality not just latency.

[04:20] Jonah Reed: good — so three axes: correctness (eval parity), latency/cost, and operational fit (VPC, SSO, audit). for correctness we recommend a seed prompt set + golden outputs; we can run evaluation harnesses and diffs.
[04:40] Priya Menon: would those tests surface tokenizer differences? sometimes TGI and OpenAI tokenizers treat emojis differently, which shifts token counts and costs.
[04:53] Jonah Reed: yes, tokenizer normalization is part of the parity checklist — we'll log tokenization and align with your current preprocessing. we also capture per-token latencies.

[07:10] Ethan Wu: technical: our vLLM instances use 16-bit quant on A100s with custom kernels; will Redwood require model re-quantization? what's the impact on quality?
[07:24] Jonah Reed: Redwood runtime supports a range of quant profiles. for Dedicated we can run your quantized model as-is if kernel compatibility exists; otherwise we recommend a minimal re-quant pass and a quick quality sweep. there are tradeoffs — smaller precision lowers cost but risks small quality difference.

[09:05] Maya Patel: hosted vs dedicated vs private — quick primer: Hosted is fastest onboarding (we manage everything), Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for throughput guarantees and isolation, Private (VPC or on‑prem) gives you full network control and on-prem options for regulated PII. which of those are you leaning to?
[09:28] Ethan Wu: we want to start with Dedicated for a controlled eval and then move to Private VPC if we like the results. need to confirm SLA and audit logging.

[11:50] Marina Holt: on legal/compliance — we need SOC2 Type II evidence, encryption at rest with KMS/HSM integration, and SSO with our SAML IdP. also data retention windows and ability to delete logs on request.
[12:12] Maya Patel: we have SOC2 artifacts and KMS integrations, we can share the security pack. audit logs are configurable per route and can be forwarded to your SIEM. deletion and retention policies are supported — we'll include specifics.

[14:33] Priya Menon: when you say "prefix caching" in Redwood, how does that differ from our current KV approach in vLLM? we sometimes pin prefixes in memory to reduce startup tokens.
[14:46] Jonah Reed: good question — Redwood does automatic prefix and KV caching with eviction policies based on workload heuristics. key difference: continuous batching + shared KV across requests can produce different cache hit patterns; we'll instrument cache hit/miss and provide traces so you can compare. sometimes you see better tail latencies because of smarter batching.

[17:55] Ethan Wu: latency is key. our P50 is 90ms for short chat queries and P95 300ms. can Redwood meet that on Dedicated?
[18:08] Jonah Reed: on Dedicated with pinned model and tuned batch sizes, p50s in your range are doable; p95 depends on traffic spikes and batching heuristics — we can set SLOs and fallback policies to a faster model variant to keep the tail down.

[20:10] Carlos Diaz: networking — for Private VPC we'll need egress lock-down and private peering. can Redwood support static egress IPs for allowlisting?
[20:22] Maya Patel: yes, for Dedicated/Private we can provide static egress and peering options; for Hosted we also have allowlisting but it's less common. we'll need to confirm exact network flow for the eval.

[22:33] Samir Rao: about model versions — we need rollout controls. can we do canary and automatic rollback?
[22:41] Jonah Reed: Redwood Console supports canary, A/B, and automatic fallback policies with percent-based rollout. you can pin versions to routes and set quality/regression monitors to auto-roll back.

[24:55] Priya Menon: quality monitoring — we want regression alerts tied to prompt sets. does Redwood support that out of the box?
[25:06] Maya Patel: yes, Optimize has eval-runwatchers and regression alerts. you upload test prompts and thresholds and we monitor token-level diffs and top-k output divergences.

[27:30] Ethan Wu: a practical question — how do you handle function calling differences? our application uses structured tool calls in the chat. sometimes provider signatures differ.
[27:43] Jonah Reed: Redwood supports function/tool calling semantics and you can map your existing schemas. during parity runs we capture call outputs and signature compatibility; we can also add a shim if there are minor differences.

[29:00] Marina Holt: encryption question — does Redwood support customer-managed keys? we need KMS/HSM with key rotation policies.
[29:11] Maya Patel: yes, Private and Dedicated support CMKs (customer-managed keys) and HSM integrations; Hosted supports customer-controlled keys for some tiers, we'll include specifics in the security pack.

[31:45] Priya Menon: for the eval we'll want to run our top 200 prompts plus a longer-tail set and measure generation diffs, token counts, latency, and cost. can Redwood run that with telemetry?
[31:56] Jonah Reed: absolutely — the typical approach is: you give us prompt set + traffic profile, we spin up a Dedicated eval pool with identical model weights, run the workload (synthetic or replayed traffic), produce per-prompt diffs, tokenization reports, cost estimates, and a performance/quality dashboard.

[34:20] Ethan Wu: how long does the eval usually take? and any upfront cost?
[34:28] Maya Patel: a minimal parity sprint is about 1 week of benchmarking plus a short dry-run. we can size the pool based on your QPS. there is a professional services eval fee for reserved capacity, but we often credit it against committed Dedicated contracts.

[36:05] Carlos Diaz: are there known compatibility issues with custom kernels we should know about? our team has some CUDA patches in production.
[36:17] Jonah Reed: custom CUDA patches are tricky. we can often reproduce the workloads on our Dedicated hardware but if there are deep kernel mods we may need a brief porting exercise. part of the parity checklist is to identify any custom kernel hooks and test them early.

[38:50] Samir Rao: fallback strategy — if we see regressions, can we route specific routes back to current provider during rollout?
[38:59] Maya Patel: yes, smart routing policies can send certain routes or users to the legacy provider; Redwood supports multi-backend routing with automated fallback based on error/latency thresholds.

[41:10] Priya Menon: licensing — if we move to Dedicated, what does upgrading models look like? can we bring our tuned weights?
[41:22] Jonah Reed: you can bring your model weights; we also support pinned versions and staged upgrades. we'll discuss IP/ML licensing in the legal thread; most customers retain model IP — Redwood's role is serving.

[43:05] Maya Patel: quick recap — Redwood will send benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, and a runtime parity checklist. Lumos will share prompt set, traffic profiles, and quant configs. we'll aim to kick the Dedicated eval the week of 2028-12-18 pending legal.
[43:22] Ethan Wu: that timeline sounds good.
[43:30] Marina Holt: we'll need the SOC2 docs and KMS details before the eval.
[43:36] Maya Patel: we'll send those today.
[45:00] Maya Patel: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with action items.

Notes: transcription contains a few misheard product names (T G I transcribed as tee-gee-eye in places). some tokenization and kernel details were abbreviated in the call.
